Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images CIA CIA director John Ratcliffe reportedly on Moscow visit Unannounced trip reported by US media is said to be Ratcliffe’s first known visit to Russia as CIA chief Peter Beaumont Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The CIA director, John Ratcliffe, has made an unannounced visit to Moscow, US media reported, after flight data showed an American military aircraft flew to the Russian capital, where a US diplomatic motorcade was later spotted. CBS News quoted sources familiar with the situation as confirming Ratcliffe’s trip, saying it was his first known visit to Russia as CIA chief. Axios separately confirmed the visit, quoting a US official. The Financial Times reported that the Trump administration had asked Kyiv to pause its long-range strikes on major Russian cities during the course of the visit. There was no immediate comment from the CIA or the White House. Data from Flightradar24 showed a US military C-17 travelling from the US to Latvia and then on to Moscow. The tracker showed that the flight originated from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, best known for hosting Air Force One. The C-17 Globemaster III is a large military transport aircraft that the US air force website says can be used for strategic and tactical airlift and airdrop missions as well as aeromedical evacuations. Ratcliffe’s reported visit comes as US-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have stalled. However, earlier this month Moscow freed a former US marine detained since 2022, amid concerns about his health. The reason for the visit is unclear but the CIA has mediated in recent US-Russia detainee exchanges and was involved in the 2024 prisoner exchange that secured the release of the Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich and the marine veteran Paul Whelan. Some speculation has focused on the war in Iran, which remains a bone of contention between Moscow and Washington. On Monday the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced a new economic sanctions strategy designed to isolate Iran . Photograph: The Rotherham NHS Foundation Trust View image in fullscreen Dolly Parton with newborn Emma, the first baby in Rotherham to receive a book from the Imagination Library programme. Photograph: The Rotherham NHS Foundation Trust Dolly Parton ‘In walked this big bundle of energy’: the day Dolly Parton came to Rotherham Country star came to South Yorkshire town in 2007 for UK launch of the Imagination Library, her book donation scheme Esther Addley Sat 29 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google S hane Jarman was up a ladder decorating a Christmas tree at the school where he was deputy headteacher when he got a call asking him to come to Rotherham hospital ASAP. It was December 2007 and Jarman’s wife, Claire, had given birth the previous day to their first child, a girl called Emma, so of course he rushed to the phone. All was well, he was told, but that “everything would become clear” when he got to the hospital. Once there, his wife told him – somewhat unexpectedly – that they were going to meet Dolly Parton. “And literally within what felt like five minutes,” he recalled, “there were great camera flashes , lots of noise, lots of clicking and in walked this real big bundle of energy.” View image in fullscreen Shane Jarman and his wife, Claire, watch as Dolly Parton holds newborn Emma. Photograph: The Rotherham NHS Foundation Trust Jarman said that as his wife handed over their tiny 4lb 6oz baby to the country star, “all I remember is seeing Dolly Parton with my little girl’s head in her hand and these great big red nails”. Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her? | Margaret Sullivan Read more Was he a little nervous about the nails? “I was very nervous about the nails to be quite honest.” Parton was in the South Yorkshire former mining and steelworking town – not principally known for its razzle-dazzle – for the British launch of the Imagination Library, the book donation programme the musician had started in her Tennessee home of Sevier County a little over a decade earlier, and which she had been invited to extend to children in Yorkshire. View image in fullscreen Dolly Parton performs at the launch of her children’s literacy scheme in Rotherham. Photograph: Rui Vieira/PA If Rotherham – or at least a gathering of local dignitaries that assembled later in a disused steelworks – was a little bemused by the singer, Parton knew places like this, and of course knew how to charm. “I gotta make sure I say your town name right – it’s Rother’m?” she said, flattening the famous southern twang to something approximating flat Yorkshire vowels. “Did I get it right? I’ve been practising because it don’t look like that on paper. In the States, anything that’s h-a-m we have to say Rother- ham .” Among the torrent of tributes to the entertainer, businesswoman and philanthropist since her death on Monday, Rotherham too has been remembering the impact of a woman who, for all her own glamour, cared deeply about places that had a little less of it. Parton may have jested when she said she had considered buying a South Yorkshire pied-à-terre (“so you may be walking down the streets of Rotherham and see me coming out of a little cubbyhole somewhere”), but her description of the post-industrialist town as “a heart spot for me” was sincere, thanks to the similarities she saw to her own outsider upbringing. “I totally related to Rotherham,” she said some years later. “I know that it’s out in an industrial area … When they were making fun of me for going out there, I thought, you know what? Don’t make fun of me.” The scheme ensured that every child in Rotherham was posted a free book, in their own name, for each month of their life until they were five, funded partly by Parton’s foundation and partly by the local authority and other local funders. Deborah Bullivant, who took over leading the Rotherham Imagination Library shortly after Parton’s visit as part of a wider literacy drive, said that despite some initial scepticism from locals, it “changed the culture” for many. View image in fullscreen Dolly Parton meets young children at the Magna Science Adventure Centre in Rotherham in 2007. Photograph: Getty “Some people were very suspicious: Why Dolly Parton? What is this thing?” she said. “[But] can you imagine receiving a book, from registering your child’s birth, your baby in their own name receives the book every month through the letterbox? For many families who didn’t really have a background in reading, it changed the culture within their homes to being more of a reading culture and embracing books and using books and sharing books.” The fact that the literacy drive was so personal to the singer was “the best way to counter any of the suspicion or worries that people had about it”, Bullivant said. “Why is Dolly Parton doing this? Who is she? She doesn’t know about this? Well, she does. She understood she needed to drive her own work herself from scratch. She got the importance of the imagination, of reading, of telling stories.” Though the Rotherham scheme was wound up in 2015 after the council withdrew support , it would be rolled out to other places in Britain, including Doncaster, North Lincolnshire, the London borough of Southwork ( “Hello Suth’rk! This is Dolly!”) and Nottingham (which even coaxed an “Ay up me duck!” from the singer). View image in fullscreen Shane Jarman and his daughter, Emma, now 18, today. Photograph: Family Handout In total, 6.3m books have been given to children across the four UK nations since one-day-old Emma Jarman received the first one in 2007, a copy of The Tale of Peter Rabbit, which Parton autographed for her. (Globally, the figure is 300m). Emma, now 18, will shortly be going to university to study biomedical science, “and, if I know Emma, [the book] will go to university with her so that she can show her friends there,” said her father. https://krmg.com/2026/08/15/europes-tall.text: News Traffic Weather On Air Dallas Cowboys on KRMG More Events Contests Podcasts Advertising Contact Us Categories Breaking News Business Contests Entertainment Green Country Local News National News News Oklahoma News Politics Sports Station Information Top Stories Uncategorized World News Home Europe’s tallest statue of the Virgin Mary is inaugurated in a small Polish village World News Europe’s tallest statue of the Virgin Mary is inaugurated in a small Polish village by Associated Press August 15, 2026 KONOTOPIE, Poland (AP) — An enormous statue of the Virgin Mary that is believed to be Europe's tallest was inaugurated on Saturday in a small Polish village, in the presence of legendary anti-communist leader Lech Walesa. Hundreds of people took part in the consecration of the monument, which towers 55.6 meters (182 feet) over Konotopie in central Poland, the home of fewer than 150 people. While helicopters scattered miniature red roses over the crowd, priests in white robes celebrated Mass and the popular Mazowsze folk ensemble sang and danced to traditional Polish music. Advertisement The Polish statue is taller — if less dramatically located — than the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, which measures some 38 meters (125 feet) including its pedestal. Its height includes a crown-shaped 15-meter (49-foot) pedestal. It also surpasses another recent large-scale religious monument in Poland, the Christ the King statue in the western town of Swiebodzin, which was unveiled in 2010 and — complete with the mound it stands on — rises some 52 meters (170 feet) above the ground. There is a taller statue of the Virgin Mary in the Philippines, which measures some 98 meters (322 feet). But the new one in Poland is believed to be the largest of its kind in Europe. Walesa, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for his leadership of the Polish anti-communist resistance as the head of the Solidarity trade union, and was later Polish president, had a front row seat during the inauguration ceremony. “This is the end of my path,” the 82-year-old Walesa told the AP, suggesting that the causes he has long championed, including democracy and Catholic faith, are now completed. “I started with the Virgin Mary and I end with the Virgin Mary.” During his Solidarity days, Walesa famously wore a Black Madonna pin and has often credited his faith in God with giving him the strength to fight against communism. The vast majority of Poles identify as Catholic, and the Catholic church played a powerful role in public life after the fall of communism in 1989, benefiting from the prestige it earned through its support for the anti-communist opposition. The country is the homeland of St. John Paul II , who reigned as pope from 1978 until his death in 2005. A huge statue of him — but much smaller than the one of Mary — was unveiled over a decade ago in the city of Czestochowa. The influence of religion in public life has gradually declined in recent years, particularly among younger people and in urban areas. However, the Catholic church remains influential, especially in rural communities and among older generations. “I cannot help but notice the weakening of the institution of the church, a withdrawal of specific social categories from Catholicism, and this hurts me,” Bishop Wiesław Mering, a Polish Roman Catholic prelate who attended the ceremony, told the AP. “The history of Christianity has ups and downs but this place is a reminder that Mary won't give up on Poland,” the bishop said. The statue was commissioned by local millionaires Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. The couple live in a small palace a few kilometers (miles) from Konotopie. Roman Karkosik, an entrepreneur whose ventures included plastic-bottle manufacturing in the 1990s, amassed a fortune through investments on the Warsaw Stock Exchange to became one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals. The couple have said the monument is an expression of their gratitude to God. “The statue will be for all people,” Grażyna Karkosik told AP. “Each of us coming to see it will think more deeply about their own lives, not only about God.” Local authorities hope the monument will become both a major pilgrimage site and a tourist destination. The statue features a viewing platform built inside its pedestal. ___ Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. Beállítom Közleményben jelentette be a közmédia átmeneti vezetése hétfőn, hogy a szervezet átvilágításakor előkerült információk alapján feljelentést tesz, mert szerintük ebből kiderült, hogyan állt az elmúlt években politikai felügyelet alatt a közmédia, és milyen szerepet töltött be az intézmény irányításában a papíron tanácsadóként szerződtetett Várhegyi Attila Fideszhez köthető politikus és üzletember. A közleményhez egy dokumentumot is csatoltak néhány példával arról, hogyan szólt bele Várhegyi személyi és operatív kérdésekbe a közmédiánál. A dokumentum szerint a közmédia dolgozói közül sokan emlegettek egy „ötödik emelet” nevű láthatatlan intézményt az MTVA négyemeletes székházában, a most feltárt adatok alapján pedig a jelenlegi vezetés azt állítja, hogy ez az „ötödik emelet” maga Várhegyi volt. Egészen konkrétan azt állítják, hogy Várhegyi Attila bizonyos meghatározó területeken nem egyszerűen tanácsokat adott, hanem ténylegesen irányította a közmédia működését. Papp Dániel vezérigazgató és más vezetők pedig állítólag nemcsak folyamatosan beszámoltak neki a legapróbb ügyekről, hanem szövegeket és döntési javaslatokat küldtek hozzá, megvárták a jóváhagyását, és rendre végrehajtották az utasításait is. A dokumentum szerint az összefonódás korábban is megjelent már, de Várhegyi hivatalosan 2019-ben jelent meg tanácsadóként a szervezetnél, a szerződését pedig aztán évről évre meghosszabbították, amivel 2023-tól egyébként havi nettó 3,5 millió forintot kapott. A dokumentumban konkrét példák is szerepelnek, például arról, hogyan szólt bele Várhegyi a személyes döntésekbe: egy alkalommal állítólag úgy reagált Szöllősi Györgynek és Papp Dánielnek egy lehetséges igazolási ötletre, hogy „ezt a buzit idehozni????”. Emellett állítólag beleszólt például abba, hogy mi legyen az év szava, vagy ki legyen az év embere – Trump és Kurtág közül itt Kurtágot hozta ki győztesnek –, és azt is állítja a dokumentum, hogy valójában a Tisza sajtósaival is ő levelezett, csak a levelek szignózását és elküldését bízta rá Papp Dánielre. Gulyás Gergely, Miniszterelnökséget vezető miniszter is Várhegyihez fordult, ha akart valamit a közmédiától, a miniszter kabinetjétől egyenesen neki küldtek például panaszlevelet az orosz nyelvű híradóról. Egy heti témalistára pedig egyszer annyit reagált a dokumentum szerint, hogy „Ukrajna és háború minden mennyiségben”. Az is felmerült a dokumentumban, hogy a Telex kérdéseinél egy idő után egy visszatérő sablon alkalmazását írta elő, benne azzal, hogy a válasz előtt azt kell kérni tőlünk, hogy áruljuk el, kik finanszíroznak bennünket, és kinek az érdekéből kérdezünk. Ezt a sablont állítólag maga Várhegyi fogalmazta meg, és mindenkit arra buzdított, hogy a „szokásos választ” küldje el aktualizálva. Ilyen sablon valóban létezett, tavaly májusban kaptuk meg először a közmédiától, amikor megkérdeztük, miért támogatják Káel Csaba filmügyi kormánybiztos készülő filmjét, a Magyar menyegzőt, és pontosan mennyi közpénzt adnak rá, de később egy másik ügynél is csak ennyit reagált az MTVA . Arról, hogy ez miért durva szereptévesztés, korábban ebben a cikkben írtunk . Várhegyi neve nem most merült fel először a közmédiával összefüggésben: ahogy az a dokumentumban is szerepel, a független sajtó korábban is próbálta már bemutatni a közmédia és az ő viszonyát. Áprilisban, pár nappal a választás után az MTVA Kunigunda utcai központjában tartott állománygyűlésen is felmerült a neve, egy újságíró kérdezett rá arra, hogy milyen szerkesztői szabadság az, amikor egy aznapi anyagból kizárólag Várhegyi Attila és Rogán Antal nevét húzzák ki.
